raw_case_text:
A 46-year-old male patient, a native of district Gorakhpur, Uttar Pradesh state, India, in October 2017 presented to us with complaints of a painless progressive swelling in the left side of the abdomen with abdominal distension for the last 8 years. The swelling was not associated with any symptom therefore the patient did not seek any medical attention for the same; however, for the last 2 years, the swelling has increased considerably as per the patient and causes dragging discomfort. It was not associated with any bladder or bowel complaints or any other systemic symptoms like fever, weight loss, or loss of appetite. Apart from dragging discomfort, there was no history of anorexia, paroxysmal hypertension, tachycardia, headache, perspiration, or palpitations. The socioeconomic status was lower middle (class III) as per modified Kuppuswamy scale, and the patient was a farmer by profession. On abdominal examination, there was a large, firm swelling of size around 20 x 15 cm occupying the left upper and lower quadrant (Fig. 1). It was non-tender and dull on percussion. The scrotum and testis were normal and there was no pedal edema or lymphadenopathy. A provisional clinical diagnosis of pseudo-pancreatic cyst was made.
Blood and laboratory investigations were within normal limits. Abdominal contrast-enhanced computed tomography was suggestive of a thin-walled hypodense cystic mass of size 25.7 x 15 x 14.3 cm in the left side of the abdomen extending from the lesser sac till the left iliac fossa. The lesion was compressing the body and tail of the pancreas. It was also displacing the head of the pancreas, stomach, first and second parts of the duodenum, small bowel loops, abdominal aorta, and superior mesenteric vessels to the right side. It was compressing the left ureter causing mild hydro-ureteronephrosis. The head of the pancreas was mildly bulky but there was no focal lesion and no evidence of free fluid or lymph nodes in the abdomen suggesting a possible diagnosis of cystic pancreatic lymphangioma (Fig. 2a, b). Twenty-four-hour urinary metanephrines were also done to rule out a cystic retroperitoneal paraganglioma and the test was negative. The diagnostic aspiration of cyst fluid (done in December 2017) revealed a total cell count of 85 cells/mm3 with 60% lymphocytes and 40% neutrophils whereas glucose was 45 mg/dl, protein 4.5 g/L, and amylase 24 U/L. The culture of cyst fluid was sterile and malignant cytology was negative.
The patient posed to us a diagnostic dilemma and we were unable to reach a definite diagnosis even after extensive investigations. The patient was planned for exploration with a probable diagnosis of pancreatic pseudocyst or lymphangioma. The patient was operated on February 2018, on exploration, and there was a cystic mass of size 25 x 15 x 15 cm (Fig. 3), which was present in the retroperitoneum pushing the small and large bowel loops anteriorly and to the right. The ureter and gonadal vessels were compressed posteriorly by the mass. Cranially, it was pushing the stomach and pancreas to the right, but there was no obvious connection with the pancreas. There were no obvious dilated lymphatics in the retroperitoneum.
Histopathology of the cyst revealed a unilocular cyst with walls composed of fibro-collagenous tissue lined by flattened epithelium and focal areas of calcification along with a few fragments of microfilaria (Fig. 4). The features were suggestive of a lymphatic cyst of filarial origin. The postoperative recovery of the patient was uneventful and was given diethylcarbamazine therapy (100 mg t.i.d. for 3 weeks). Further, filariasis immunochromatographic test (ICT) by Alere  BinaxNOW  Filariasis kit for Wucheria bancrofti was positive. Ultrasound of the scrotum, groin, and lower extremity was reviewed again for possible adult worm and, however, was negative. The patient was doing fine up to 8 months of follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 46-year-old Indian male farmer presenting with an 8-year history of a progressively enlarging left abdominal swelling causing dragging discomfort over the past 2 years.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient noticed a painless left abdominal mass 8 years prior that enlarged substantially over the preceding 2 years, producing a chronic dragging abdominal discomfort without bowel, urinary, or constitutional symptoms.
subjective.past_medical_history: Farmer from Gorakhpur district, Uttar Pradesh, India (lower-middle socioeconomic status).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for left abdominal swelling and dragging discomfort; negative for fever, weight loss, anorexia, bowel/bladder dysfunction, paroxysmal hypertension, headache, diaphoresis, or palpitations.

objective.physical_examination: Abdominal examination revealed a large, firm, non-tender mass measuring ~20 x 15 cm occupying the left upper and lower quadrants that was dull to percussion. Scrotum and testes were normal without pedal edema or peripheral lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine hematological and biochemical investigations and 24-hour urinary metanephrines were normal. Scrotal, groin, and lower-extremity Doppler ultrasound was negative for adult filarial worms.
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed a 25.7 x 15 x 14.3 cm thin-walled hypodense retroperitoneal cystic mass extending from the lesser sac to the left iliac fossa, displacing the pancreas, stomach, duodenum, bowel loops, and great vessels to the right and compressing the left ureter with mild hydroureteronephrosis. Ultrasound-guided cyst fluid aspiration showed 85 cells/mm3 (60% lymphocytes, 40% neutrophils), glucose 45 mg/dL, protein 4.5 g/L, amylase 24 U/L, negative cytology, and sterile bacterial culture.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed retroperitoneal filarial lymphatic cyst caused by Wuchereria bancrofti, established by surgical excision histopathology (fibro-collagenous cyst wall with calcifications and microfilarial fragments) and positive Alere BinaxNOW Filariasis immunochromatographic test (ICT). Pancreatic pseudocyst and retroperitoneal paraganglioma were ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Underwent exploratory laparotomy with complete excision of the 25 x 15 x 15 cm retroperitoneal cyst, followed by oral diethylcarbamazine (DEC) 100 mg three times daily for 3 weeks. Postoperative recovery was uneventful with no recurrence at 8-month follow-up.
